items.stem: Globalisation refers to
options: the use of a single world currency
the increasing integration of national economies through trade, capital flows, technology and migration
items.answer: the increasing integration of national economies through trade, capital flows, technology and migration
items.markingKey: Growing interdependence.

items.stem: Explain two causes of globalisation.
items.answer: Improvements in transport (containers, air freight) and ICT; trade liberalisation through the WTO and trading blocs; deregulation of financial markets; growth of MNCs; opening of China and other economies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain how the growth of the internet has contributed to globalisation of the brewing industry.
items.answer: Lower communication costs allow firms to coordinate global supply chains, sell to customers worldwide and outsource services; information flows freely, increasing competition.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower communication costs; 1 mark: global supply chains/markets [2]

items.stem: Umbria Nova has exports of $200 billion, imports of $350 billion and GDP of $1500 billion. Calculate the trade openness ratio.

Istrana: exports $200bn, imports $350bn, GDP $1000bn. Ten years later exports have risen 50%, imports 60% and GDP 30%. Calculate the openness ratio at both dates and explain what the change suggests about globalisation and one risk for Istrana.
items.answer: Openness 55% → 66.2%: trade has grown faster than GDP, so Istrana is more integrated into the world economy. Risk: greater exposure to external shocks (world recessions, commodity prices), competition for domestic firms.
items.markingKey: Ratios at both dates [2]; interpretation [1]; risk [1].

items.stem: Extract: Fendaria’s trade openness ratio has risen from 40% to 85% since it joined a regional customs union with Loristan and Gorvania. Manufacturing exports have grown rapidly, but some domestic farmers complain that they cannot compete with imports. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the openness ratio. (b) Explain why farmers may lose from the customs union.
items.answer: (a) 112.5% (b) Removal of tariffs exposes them to lower-cost partner producers; prices fall.

items.stem: Which is a cause of globalisation?
items.answer: Falling transport and communication costs
items.markingKey: Containerisation, internet, trade liberalisation, deregulation of capital flows.

Calvania: exports $150bn, imports $350bn, GDP $1000bn. Ten years later exports have risen 50%, imports 60% and GDP 30%. Calculate the openness ratio at both dates and explain what the change suggests about globalisation and one risk for Calvania.
items.answer: Openness 50% → 60.4%: trade has grown faster than GDP, so Calvania is more integrated into the world economy. Risk: greater exposure to external shocks (world recessions, commodity prices), competition for domestic firms.

items.stem: Trade in Ostrelia has doubled as a share of GDP in 30 years. To what extent do you agree that globalisation is mainly the result of technological change rather than government policy?
items.answer: Arguments for: Transport and ICT innovations lowered trade costs dramatically. Arguments against / evaluation: Trade liberalisation, WTO, capital deregulation and opening of economies were essential; both interact. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Trade creation occurs when
options: imports from a low-cost non-member are replaced by higher-cost imports from a member
tariffs are raised on all imports
joining a trading bloc replaces higher-cost domestic production with lower-cost imports from a member
items.answer: joining a trading bloc replaces higher-cost domestic production with lower-cost imports from a member
items.markingKey: Welfare gain.

items.stem: Distinguish between trade creation and trade diversion, giving an example of each.
items.answer: Creation: a member switches from high-cost domestic production to cheaper imports from a partner after internal tariffs are removed. Diversion: a member switches from a cheaper non-member supplier to a dearer partner because the common external tariff makes non-member goods more expensive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition, 1 mark each example [4]

items.stem: Explain two benefits of a common market beyond those of a customs union.
items.answer: Free movement of labour and capital allows resources to move to their most productive uses; larger market gives economies of scale; harmonised regulations lower costs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Kestria can buy tyres from domestic producers at $30, from a neighbouring country at $28 and from the rest of the world at $22 (prices before tariffs). Kestria applies a 60% tariff on all imports. It then forms a customs union with the neighbour, removing the tariff on its goods but keeping the tariff on the rest of the world. Which supplier is cheapest after the customs union is formed?
items.answer: The partner country
items.markingKey: Prices after: domestic 30, partner 28, rest of world 35.2 → the partner country.

items.stem: Valdoria can buy televisions from domestic producers at $32, from a neighbouring country at $24 and from the rest of the world at $20 (prices before tariffs). Valdoria applies a 40% tariff on all imports. It then forms a customs union with the neighbour, removing the tariff on its goods but keeping the tariff on the rest of the world. Calculate the price from each source before and after the customs union, identify the cheapest source in each case, and state whether this is trade creation or trade diversion. Explain the welfare effect.
items.answer: Before: domestic $32, partner $33.6, world $28 → the rest of the world. After: domestic $32, partner $24, world $28 → the partner country. Result: trade diversion. Welfare loss: supply moves from the lowest-cost world producer ($20) to a higher-cost partner ($24); the government also loses tariff revenue.
items.markingKey: Tariff-inclusive prices [2]; cheapest source before and after [1]; classification [1]; welfare explanation [1].

items.stem: Esteria can buy tyres from domestic producers at $30, from a neighbouring country at $28 and from the rest of the world at $22 (prices before tariffs). Esteria applies a 60% tariff on all imports. It then forms a customs union with the neighbour, removing the tariff on its goods but keeping the tariff on the rest of the world. Calculate the price from each source before and after the customs union, identify the cheapest source in each case, and state whether this is trade creation or trade diversion. Explain the welfare effect.
items.answer: Before: domestic $30, partner $44.8, world $35.2 → domestic producers. After: domestic $30, partner $28, world $35.2 → the partner country. Result: trade creation. Welfare gain: resources move from higher-cost domestic production to a lower-cost producer.
items.markingKey: Tariff-inclusive prices [2]; cheapest source before and after [1]; classification [1]; welfare explanation [1].

items.stem: Extract: Quentara’s trade openness ratio has risen from 35% to 70% since it joined a regional customs union with Gorvania and Tarvia. Manufacturing exports have grown rapidly, but some domestic farmers complain that they cannot compete with imports. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the openness ratio. (b) Explain the difference between trade creation and trade diversion in this customs union.
items.answer: (a) 100% (b) Creation: cheaper partner imports replace domestic output; diversion: dearer partner imports replace cheaper non-member imports due to the common external tariff.

items.stem: Explain why globalisation may increase income inequality within developed countries.
items.answer: Low-skilled workers face competition from imports and offshoring, lowering their wages, while high-skilled workers and capital owners gain from larger markets.

items.stem: Over 20 years of rapid globalisation in Halvoria, manufacturing’s share of employment fell from 28% to 12% and services rose from 60% to 75%. Real wages of low-skilled workers rose by 5% in total while those of graduates rose by 30%. Calculate the percentage change in manufacturing’s share of employment and analyse how globalisation could explain these trends.
items.answer: Manufacturing share fell by 16 percentage points (-57.1%). Offshoring and import competition shifted manufacturing to lower-cost countries; growth of tradable services; rising demand for skilled workers raised their relative wages, increasing inequality.
items.markingKey: % change [1]; offshoring/comparative advantage [1]; skill-biased effect on wages [1]; inequality conclusion [1].

items.stem: A clothing factory in Valdoria closes after production moves to Jovania. Explain how this illustrates a consequence of globalisation.
items.answer: Firms relocate production to lower-cost countries (comparative advantage, offshoring), causing structural unemployment in the original country but jobs and growth in the new location.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relocation; 1 mark: structural unemployment/gains elsewhere [2]

items.stem: Over 20 years of rapid globalisation in Tarvia, manufacturing’s share of employment fell from 25% to 12% and services rose from 60% to 72%. Real wages of low-skilled workers rose by 5% in total while those of graduates rose by 30%. Calculate the percentage change in manufacturing’s share of employment and analyse how globalisation could explain these trends.
items.answer: Manufacturing share fell by 13 percentage points (-52%). Offshoring and import competition shifted manufacturing to lower-cost countries; growth of tradable services; rising demand for skilled workers raised their relative wages, increasing inequality.
items.markingKey: % change [1]; offshoring/comparative advantage [1]; skill-biased effect on wages [1]; inequality conclusion [1].

items.stem: Over 20 years of rapid globalisation in Sundara, manufacturing’s share of employment fell from 25% to 16% and services rose from 62% to 75%. items.stem: Several factories in Pelora have moved production overseas in the last decade. (a) Explain how globalisation affects employment in developed economies. (b) To what extent do you agree that globalisation has harmed workers in developed economies?
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Offshoring, import competition, lower wages for low-skilled. (b) Case for the view: Offshoring, import competition, lower wages for low-skilled. Case against / evaluation: Cheaper goods raise real incomes, new jobs in services and exports, retraining; technology also responsible. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.
